title: Indexes (advanced)
summary: Why foreign keys need an index and how composite index order matters.
body:
Why foreign keys need an index and how composite index order matters.

Why it matters: Postgres creates indexes for PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE automatically — never for foreign keys. Every join, every `WHERE author_id = ?` and every ON DELETE check on the parent then scans the child table.

SQL ↔ ORM: SQLAlchemy mapped_column(..., index=True) / Index(...). Prisma @@index([field]). SQL CREATE INDEX name ON table (col).
why: Postgres creates indexes for PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE automatically — never for foreign keys. Every join, every `WHERE author_id = ?` and every ON DELETE check on the parent then scans the child table.
objectives: Know that only the LEADING column of a composite index serves single-column lookups.
Read an index from the schema diagram.
pitfalls: Composite index (title, author_id) for lookups by author_id.
Indexing every column — each index slows writes.
mappingNotes: SQLAlchemy mapped_column(..., index=True) / Index(...). Prisma @@index([field]). SQL CREATE INDEX name ON table (col).

exercise.prompt: Add @@index([authorId]) so lookups and joins on author_id do not scan the whole table.
exercise.hint: Prisma does not create FK indexes on PostgreSQL either — add @@index explicitly.

wrongSolutions.label: no @@index
